title: The Umbrella We Didn't Need
author: Anonymous, 23
content:
It had stopped raining ten minutes before we left the café. I know because I checked. I checked twice. But you opened the umbrella anyway and held it over both of us, and I didn't say anything, and you didn't say anything, and we walked the whole length of Linking Road under a sky that was completely, embarrassingly dry.

People looked at us. An uncle selling corn laughed out loud. A group of college kids pointed and whispered. You said, very seriously, "It might start again," and I said, "Yeah, you never know," and neither of us believed it for a second.

The umbrella was small, the cheap kind with one bent spoke, so our shoulders kept bumping. Every time they did, you apologised, and every time you apologised, you somehow ended up a little closer. By the time we reached the signal, there was no space left to apologise for.

I think that's when I knew. Not at dinner, not when you remembered I hate coriander, not when you sent me that song at midnight with no message, just the link. It was the umbrella. It was the fact that you needed an excuse to stand that close to me, and you were willing to look a little stupid in front of all of Bandra to have one.

At the auto stand you finally closed it. You shook it out like it was soaking wet, which it wasn't, and handed it to me. "Keep it," you said. "For next time." I asked what next time. You just smiled and got into your auto, and I stood there holding a dry umbrella like it was the most precious thing I owned.

We've been together two years now. That umbrella lives by our front door. The spoke is still bent. You still open it when it isn't raining, on our evening walks, outside the cinema, once even inside a mall, which got us a very confused look from a security guard. I still let you.

Some days I catch myself checking the forecast and hoping for clouds, just so we can pretend we need shelter from them. Most days I realise we never needed the rain. We only ever needed the excuse.

title: Grocery List, Second Draft
author: Anonymous, 27
content:
Nobody tells you that love eventually looks like a grocery list.

Not in a sad way. In the best way. Last week I found a note on the fridge in your handwriting: milk, eggs, the spicy chips she likes (not the green ones, the red ones), bread, call mom. I stood in the kitchen holding it like it was a love letter, because honestly, it was.

When we started dating, love was the big stuff. The long drives with the windows down. The first trip to Goa where we missed the last bus and walked four kilometres in the dark, laughing the whole way. The night we talked on the terrace until the birds started and the neighbour aunty came up to hang her clothes and found us still there. I thought that was the whole thing. I thought the fireworks were the point.

Now it's you knowing which chips. It's me buying the toothpaste you like even though it costs forty rupees more. It's you texting "reached?" every single time I travel, even for the twenty-minute ride to my sister's place. It's the way you leave the last piece of chocolate in the fridge and pretend you forgot about it, every time, for three years.

It's you warming my side of the bed with a hot water bottle in December without saying anything. It's me learning to make your mother's rajma, failing four times, and you eating all four versions and saying each one was the best. It's arguing about whose turn it is to take out the trash and then both doing it together anyway, in our slippers, at eleven at night.

My friends sometimes ask if it gets boring. I understand why they ask. From the outside it probably looks small. No grand gestures, no surprise flights, no flowers delivered to the office.

But I've started to think love isn't the fireworks. It's what's left after the fireworks, when the sky is quiet and someone is still standing next to you, holding your hand, pointing out the stars.

The fireworks were beautiful. I'll never forget them. But I'd trade every single one for this: a list on the fridge, the red chips, not the green ones, written by someone who was paying attention all along.

title: Voice Note, 1:12 AM
author: Anonymous, 21
content:
You sent a seven-minute voice note at 1:12 AM and I have listened to it more times than I'm willing to admit.

It's not even about anything. You start by telling me about your cousin's wedding plans and how your aunt wants a theme, and the theme is "royal," and nobody knows what that means. Then you get distracted by a cat outside your window that is apparently "judging you." Then you spend almost a full minute trying to remember the name of a movie we should watch together. You never find it. Somewhere around minute five you yawn and say, "Okay, I should sleep," and then talk for two more minutes anyway.

I play it when I'm walking to class. I play it when the metro is too crowded to think and someone's elbow is in my ribs. I played it last night with the volume low, lying in the dark, just to hear you laugh at your own joke about the cat. You have this laugh that starts as a snort and then gives up and becomes a real laugh. I didn't know I'd been waiting my whole life to hear it.

We've known each other for three months. We haven't even been on a proper date. Just coffee twice and one long walk after a class got cancelled. But somewhere in those voice notes I started to feel like I know you. Not the you that everyone sees. The 1 AM you. The one who's sleepy and a bit silly and talks to cats.

My friends tease me. They say I'm too far gone. They've started calling you "Voice Note" instead of your name. They're right. I am too far gone. I didn't know a person's voice could feel like a place you go to rest.

I've started saving them in a folder. There are forty-one now. I know that's a lot. I'm not going to tell you.

The movie was Before Sunrise, by the way. I figured it out at 2 AM, sitting straight up in bed like I'd solved a murder. I haven't told you yet. I'm saving it as an excuse to call. Maybe this weekend. Maybe I'll ask if you want to watch it together.

Maybe I'll finally say it out loud.

title: The First Time I Introduced You
author: Anonymous, 25
content:
I had rehearsed it for a week. "Ma, this is the friend I told you about." Friend. As if she didn't already know. As if my mother hasn't been reading my face since before I could talk.

You were more nervous than me, which I didn't think was possible. You called me three times that morning. Should you bring flowers or sweets? Should you wear a kurta or a shirt? Should you touch her feet or would that be too much? I said just be yourself, and you said, "That's exactly what I'm worried about."

You wore the blue shirt I said looked good on you, which I now realise was a strategic decision. You brought sweets from the shop near your house, the one with the long queue, and you stood in that queue for forty minutes because I once mentioned, months ago, in passing, that my mom loves their kaju katli. I didn't even remember saying it.

She made you sit on the good sofa, the one with the plastic cover that nobody is allowed to sit on. My brother noticed and raised his eyebrows at me from the doorway. She asked about your job, your parents, your hometown, whether you eat properly, whether you can cook. You answered everything like it was a job interview, sitting very straight, hands on your knees.

Then she asked if you wanted more tea, and you said, "Only if you're making it for yourself too, aunty," and I watched her decide, right there, that she liked you. I saw it happen. Something in her shoulders softened.

After that it was easy. She showed you my childhood photos, including the terrible one with the bowl haircut. You laughed so hard you had to put your cup down. She packed leftovers for you in three different containers when you left.

After you left she didn't say anything for a long time. She just collected the cups and walked to the kitchen. I followed her, waiting. Then, washing the cups, without looking at me, she said: "He holds the door for you. Good."

That's all. A few quiet words of approval. I went to the bathroom and cried for ten minutes, and I've never been happier in my whole life.

title: Blinding Lights on the Expressway
author: Anonymous, 24
content:
There's a stretch of the expressway around 2 AM where it's just you, the sodium lights, and the occasional truck that passes like a ship in the dark. That's where I go when my head is too loud.

I put on Blinding Lights, roll the windows down, and drive until the city thins out. I don't go anywhere. That's the point. Some people need a destination. I need a direction. Forward, away, anything but sitting still in an apartment that's too quiet.

She used to sit in the passenger seat with her feet on the dashboard, painting her nails in the light from the phone, singing the synth parts badly on purpose. She'd say, "One more song and then we turn back," and we never turned back after one more song. We'd end up at a dhaba sixty kilometres away, eating parathas at 4 AM, her nail polish still drying, the truck drivers staring at us like we'd landed from another planet.

She said this was her favourite version of me. Night me. The one who didn't check emails, who drove with one hand and held hers with the other, who laughed easily. She said day me was always somewhere else. I told her she was being dramatic. She wasn't.

It's been eight months. I still don't let anyone else sit in that seat. My friends think it's weird. One of them tried to get in last week and I made up a story about the seat belt being broken. Maybe it is weird. But some spaces stay shaped like a person long after they leave.

There's still a tiny drop of pink nail polish on the dashboard. I've tried to clean it twice. I stopped both times.

I turn around at the toll plaza. Always the same one. The guy in the booth knows my car now. He nodded at me last week, like he understood something. Maybe he does. Maybe everyone who drives at 2 AM is running from the same kind of quiet.

On the way back the city slowly fills up again. Lights, buildings, the first milk vans. The song ends. I don't play it again. I drive home in silence and tell myself that tomorrow I'll stay in. I never do.

title: Save Your Tears (For a Party)
author: Anonymous, 26
content:
I saw you at Riya's birthday. You were laughing at something across the room, wearing that black jacket you stole from me in the second month and never gave back.

I had prepared for this. I'd heard you might come. I had a whole version of myself ready: the one who's doing great, who has a new job and a new haircut and doesn't check your Instagram stories at night. I practised her in the mirror. I wore her like a costume. I even arrived late on purpose so it wouldn't look like I was waiting.

I said hi. You said hi. We talked about the weather, and work, and whether Riya's new flat was too far from the metro, like two people who had never fallen asleep on the same phone call. Like two people who hadn't once planned a trip to Ladakh down to the day, the bike, the playlist.

You asked if I was seeing someone. I said, "Kind of," which was a lie. You nodded slowly and said, "That's good. You deserve that." And I hated how kind you sounded. I wanted you to be a little bit jealous. I wanted you to be a little bit sorry.

Then the DJ played Save Your Tears and we both looked up at the same time. Of course he did. Of course it was that song, out of every song in the world. It was the song from that night in Pune when the power went out and we danced in the dark using your phone as a speaker.

You gave me a small smile, the one that used to mean "I know what you're thinking," and for one second the costume slipped. Just one second. But you saw it. I know you saw it.

I went to the balcony. Not to cry. Just to breathe somewhere that didn't have you in it. The city was loud below me. Someone was arguing on the phone two balconies down. I stood there until the song ended and the next one started, something fast and forgettable.

When I came back inside, you'd left. Your glass was still on the table, half full. I don't know why that hurt the most. Maybe because you always used to finish everything. Every plate, every movie, every bottle.

Everything, except us.

title: After Hours at the Petrol Pump
author: Anonymous, 22
content:
The only place open at 3 AM in my part of the city is the petrol pump with the tiny convenience store. I end up there more often than I'd like to admit.

It started during exams. I couldn't sleep, couldn't study, couldn't stay in my room with my thoughts going around like a ceiling fan. So I walked. And the petrol pump was the only lit thing on the road, glowing white and green like a spaceship that had landed between a closed tyre shop and an empty bus stop.

It's a strange little world at that hour. A cab driver eating Maggi on the bonnet of his car. Two college guys arguing about whether a girl "meant it" when she said goodnight with a full stop instead of an emoji. A delivery rider asleep sitting up, helmet still on, phone glowing in his lap with an order he's waiting for. An old man who buys one cigarette and smokes it very slowly, looking at the sky.

And me, buying a cold coffee I don't need, because sitting at home with my thoughts felt worse than spending eighty rupees.

The store guy plays the same playlist every night from a small speaker behind the counter. Somewhere around 3:20, it's always The Weeknd. I don't think he even notices anymore. But every time In Your Eyes comes on, the cab driver mouths the words, and the college guys stop arguing, and the old man taps his foot. For three and a half minutes nobody in that tiny fluorescent store is alone.

We never talk. Not really. We just nod when we arrive and nod again when we leave. Once, the cab driver offered me a bite of his Maggi, and I took it, and that's the closest any of us have come to a conversation.

But I've started to think of them as my night people: strangers who also couldn't sleep, also needed somewhere bright to stand until the feeling passed.

Exams are over now. I sleep better. But some nights, around three, I still put on my slippers and walk there. Not for the coffee. Just to check they're all okay. Just to be okay together, for one song.

title: The Hills Have Your Number
author: Anonymous, 28
content:
You only ever called after midnight. I should have noticed that sooner.

Daytime you was busy, distant, always "in a meeting" or "with family" or "just tired today, talk later?" Later never came in daylight. But at 1 AM you'd text "you up?" and I'd pretend I wasn't waiting for exactly that, phone in hand, screen brightness all the way down so I wouldn't wake my roommate.

You'd say things in the dark you never said in daylight. That you missed me. That I was the only one who really understood you. That you were sorry about last time, and the time before that. That things would be different once work calmed down, once your family stopped asking questions, once you figured things out.

Work never calmed down. You know that. I know that now too.

It took me a year to understand that I was loving someone who only existed between midnight and 4 AM. The rest of the time I was dating a ghost who replied with "haha" and left me on read for days and forgot my birthday until 11 PM, when you sent a single cake emoji and nothing else.

My best friend stopped asking about you. She didn't say anything. She just started changing the subject when I brought you up, and I understood that silence was her way of telling me something I wasn't ready to hear.

The worst part is that the midnight version of you was real. I believe that. I think you did mean those things, for the hour you were saying them. But a person who only loves you at night is not loving you. They're just lonely in the dark, and you happen to be awake.

Last week your name lit up my phone at 1:40. I watched it ring. I watched it stop. I watched the "you up?" arrive, then "hello??", then "ok whatever."

I put the phone face down and played The Hills loud enough that I couldn't hear myself wanting to answer. Then I played it again. Then I slept, properly, for the first time in weeks.

I didn't reply. It's the smallest victory, and the biggest thing I've done all year.

title: Seen at 11:48
author: Anonymous, 20
content:
Seen at 11:48.

That's it. That's the whole story. I sent you a long message about how my day went, the funny thing my professor said about pigeons, a meme I knew you'd like because it was about your favourite show, and a small, careful question at the end: "Free this weekend?"

I rewrote that question six times. "Want to hang out?" felt too eager. "We should catch up" felt too formal. "Free this weekend?" seemed casual enough that if you said no, I could pretend it didn't matter.

Seen at 11:48. It's now 2:15.

I've opened our chat maybe forty times. I've watched you come online and go offline. I've seen "typing..." appear once, for four seconds, and then disappear, and I've spent an hour wondering what you typed and deleted. I've seen you post a story at 12:30, a sunset from your terrace with a song I recommended to you last month, so I know you weren't asleep. I know you had your phone in your hand.

The worst part is that I'm already making excuses for you. Maybe you're tired. Maybe you're busy with family. Maybe you'll reply in the morning with a long message and a sorry and a yes. Maybe you're figuring out how to say yes without sounding too excited, the same way I figured out how to ask without sounding too hopeful.

I scroll up through our chat. It's mostly me. Long paragraphs from me, short replies from you. "Haha." "True." "Nice." Questions from me, answers from you, never questions back. I never noticed the shape of it before. It looks like a staircase where only one person is climbing.

Somewhere under all the excuses there's a quieter voice, and it's been getting louder for months. It says: you would never leave them on seen. Not for a second. Not even at 3 AM. Not even if you were busy, or tired, or sad.

And I think that's the whole difference between us.

I'm a full sentence. You're a read receipt.

I put my phone on the charger, face down. I tell myself I won't check it until morning. I check it at 2:31.

title: The Best Friend Clause
author: Anonymous, 23
content:
You call me your best friend at least once a day, and every time it feels like a door being closed very politely.

We met in the first week of college, both lost, both looking for the same classroom. You grabbed my arm and said, "Please tell me you also have no idea where Room 204 is." I didn't. We found it together, twenty minutes late. That's been us ever since. Lost, together.

I'm the first person you text when something goes wrong. I know your coffee order, your sister's name, your Netflix password, the exact way you fold your dupatta when you're nervous. I know that you pretend to like horror movies but close your eyes at every jump scare. I know you cry at the end of every Pixar film, even the bad ones.

I was there when he cancelled on you for the third time. I brought chocolate and the cheap chips you love. I said all the right things. I said, "You deserve someone who shows up," and you hugged me for a long time and said, "What would I do without you?"

I wanted to say: let me show up. Let me be the one who doesn't cancel. I've been showing up for four years. But that sentence would break the best friend clause, the unspoken contract where I get to keep you as long as I never ask for more.

So I stay. I listen to you talk about other people. I help you pick an outfit for a date that isn't with me, and tell you the green one is better, because it is. I wait up to make sure you got home safe. I tell myself that having half of you is better than losing all of you.

Your mom calls me beta. Your little brother asks me for help with maths. Everyone in your life knows me, and loves me, as exactly what I am to you. Nobody would believe it could be anything else. Sometimes I don't believe it either.

Some nights I believe that half is enough. Most nights I don't.

But I always pick up when you call. I always will. That's the clause. I signed it the day you grabbed my arm outside Room 204, and I'd sign it again.

title: I Learned Her Favourite Band
author: Anonymous, 22
content:
She mentioned a band once, in the canteen, in passing. I'd never heard of them. That night I listened to their entire discography. Twice.

I'm not proud of it. But I'm not ashamed of it either. I learned the lyrics. I found out the drummer's name, the album that "real fans" prefer, the song they never play live because the lead singer wrote it about his father. I watched a two-hour documentary about their first tour. I wasn't trying to fake anything. I genuinely wanted to love the things she loved, because I thought maybe that's how you get closer to someone: you walk into the rooms they already live in.

And the strange thing is, I did love them. Their songs were sad in a way that felt like company. I started listening to them on the bus, in the library, walking home. I'd hear a line and think, this is what she hears. This is what she feels when she puts her earphones in.

Two weeks later I casually brought it up. I'd planned the casualness for days. "Have you heard their second album?" She lit up. She actually put her phone down. We talked for an hour, about the songs, about the lyrics, about the concert she went to in Bangalore when she was sixteen. It was the best hour of the semester. Maybe the best hour of the year.

I walked back to the hostel feeling like something had begun.

The next day she said, "You'd really get along with my boyfriend, he's obsessed with them too. We should all go to a gig sometime."

I smiled. I said that's great, we should. I asked how they met. I asked what he studies. I was so polite it surprised me. Inside, something very quietly folded itself up and put itself away.

We never went to that gig. She graduated. We lost touch the way people do, slowly, without anyone deciding to.

But I still listen to that band. Not to remember her, exactly. Just because some of the songs turned out to be beautiful on their own. I guess that's what one-sided love leaves you with: a playlist you discovered for someone else that slowly, without asking, becomes yours.

title: The Wedding Card
author: Anonymous, 29
content:
The card was beautiful. Cream paper, gold lettering, a little sketch of a banyan tree. Your name and his, side by side. At the bottom, in your handwriting: "You HAVE to come. No excuses!!"

I had loved you for six years without ever saying it out loud. Through college, through your first job in Hyderabad, through your father's surgery, through that winter you cried on my shoulder in the office parking lot because your manager humiliated you in a meeting. I always thought there would be a right moment.

After exams. After you settled into the new city. After your father recovered. After this deadline, after that trip, after things calmed down. I kept moving the moment further away, like a horizon, telling myself it was patience when really it was fear.

The right moment was never coming. I know that now. Some people spend their whole lives standing at the edge of a sentence, waiting for permission to finish it.

I thought about not going. I had excuses ready. Work, a cousin's thing, a fever. But I went. Of course I went.

I wore green because you once said it suited me. I helped your mom with the decorations. I danced at your sangeet, badly, to a song we used to sing in the car. He seemed kind. That was the hardest part. I wanted him to be awful, and he was kind. He thanked me for "taking care of her all these years." I said it was nothing.

When you hugged me after the pheras and said, "I'm so glad you're here," you meant it completely, and that was the kindest and cruellest thing anyone has ever done to me.

On the drive home I finally said it. Out loud, alone in the car, on the empty highway, to no one: "I loved you." Six years late and three words short of mattering.

It didn't change anything. I didn't expect it to. But it was mine to say, and I finally said it. Then I turned on the radio, and drove, and somewhere around the toll plaza I realised I was breathing a little easier.

Maybe that's what closure is. Not an ending. Just finally letting the sentence finish.

title: Two Clocks on My Wall
author: Anonymous, 24
content:
I have two clocks on my wall. One for here. One for you, five and a half hours behind, in a city I've only seen through a phone camera.

I bought the second one the week you left. It was the cheapest one in the shop, plastic, with a ticking so loud I had to take the batteries out the first night. I put them back the next morning. I decided I'd rather hear it.

My friends think it's dramatic. Maybe it is. But I like looking up and knowing: right now you're on your way to work, earphones in, probably late. Right now you're eating that terrible sandwich from the place near your office that you keep complaining about and keep buying. Right now you're asleep, and the dark has you, and it's my turn to hold the day.

We've learned to love in the gaps. You send me good morning while I'm having lunch. I send you goodnight when you're just starting your evening. Our conversations are long, stretched threads, picked up and put down across continents, like a letter written one line at a time. Sometimes I reply to something you said six hours ago and it feels like talking to the past.

We have our rituals. Sunday calls at a time that's awkward for both of us. Watching the same sunset photos, mine at dusk and yours at noon. Ordering the same dish on the same day, a world apart, and eating it on camera.

The hardest part isn't the distance. It's the small things I can't do. I can't bring you soup when you're sick. I can't see your face when the news is bad, only a frozen, pixelated version of it while the call reconnects. I can't just sit next to you in silence, which I've realised is one of the most intimate things two people can do.

Some nights I miss you so much it feels physical, like a weight sitting on my chest. Other nights I feel strangely close to you, closer than couples who share a bed and never talk.

Forty-three days until you land. I count them on the second clock, the loud one, the one that keeps your time. Every tick is a second closer. I've stopped finding it annoying. Now it sounds like footsteps.

title: Watch Party, Lagging
author: Anonymous, 21
content:
Every Saturday we have movie night. We press play at the same second, count down on the call, "three, two, one, go," and somehow we're always out of sync by about four seconds.

We've tried everything. Watch-party apps that crash. Screen-sharing that turns every movie into a slideshow. Restarting at exactly the same time five times in a row. It doesn't matter. The four seconds always come back, like a ghost that follows us across the internet.

So I laugh at the joke, and four seconds later you laugh at the joke. I gasp at the twist, and then your gasp arrives like an echo from another room. At first it annoyed me. I used to pause and say, "Wait, wait, sync up." Now it's my favourite part. It's like hearing the same feeling twice. Like the movie is happening to both of us, just one after another.

We have rules. No spoilers, even though you always guess the ending. Snacks must be shown on camera before the movie starts. If one of us cries, the other one isn't allowed to tease, which is a rule you made after the Coco incident.

You fall asleep before the movie ends. Every single time. Even when you choose the movie. Even when you say, "No, tonight I'm definitely staying awake." I can see you on the little screen, phone tilted on the pillow, mouth slightly open, the light from your laptop flickering across your face.

I never hang up. I watch the rest of the movie alone, quietly, with the sound of you breathing six hundred kilometres away. Sometimes you mumble in your sleep. Once you said, very clearly, "no, the blue one," and I've been wondering about the blue one for months.

People ask how we do it. How do you love someone you can't touch? I don't have a good answer. I just know that when your face disappears into sleep and the call keeps running, I don't feel far from you at all. I feel like I'm keeping watch.

We've seen maybe forty movies this way. I don't know how half of them end, and you don't know how most of them end.

We've agreed to watch all of them again, properly, on the same couch, when this is over.

title: The Airport Doesn't Get Easier
author: Anonymous, 26
content:
Everyone said the goodbyes would get easier. They lied.

The arrivals are perfect. I always get there an hour early, even though I know your flight is delayed. I stand at the barrier with all the families and drivers holding name boards, and I watch the doors slide open and closed, open and closed, my heart jumping every single time.

Then I see you coming through the gate with your terrible neck pillow and your hair flattened on one side, scanning the crowd, and the moment our eyes meet the whole terminal goes quiet. You always walk faster for the last few steps. I always pretend I'm not crying.

Those first few days are like living inside a song. We cook badly. We walk everywhere. We go to the same café we went to on our first date and order the same things. We fall asleep holding hands like teenagers and wake up surprised, every morning, that the other person is actually there and not a face on a screen.

But the last night always comes. It sneaks up on us. You start folding clothes and we both pretend we're fine. We order your favourite food and don't finish it. We set an alarm that feels like a countdown and lie awake waiting for it.

At the airport there's a line painted on the floor where non-passengers have to stop. Yellow, thick, official. I hate that line more than I've ever hated anything. You walk past it and I stay behind it, and you turn around three times. I count. Always three. On the third one you wave, and then the crowd swallows you.

Then I drive home to an apartment that still smells like you. I find your hair tie on the bathroom counter, your cup still in the sink, the dent in the pillow. I sit on the floor for a while. I don't turn the lights on.

The next morning you text me from your city, "landed, miss you already," and the clocks start again.

It doesn't get easier. I've stopped expecting it to. But I've figured something out: every goodbye is one closer to the last one. One day you'll walk through that gate and there won't be a return ticket.

That's what I hold on to.

title: A Parcel With Your Hoodie
author: Anonymous, 22
content:
The parcel arrived on a Tuesday, which was the worst day of a terrible week. My presentation had gone badly. My landlord had called about the rent. It had rained all day, and I'd forgotten my umbrella, and my shoes were still wet.

I almost didn't open it. It was sitting outside my door, a little crushed at one corner, and I thought it was another thing I'd ordered at 2 AM and forgotten about. I left it on the table for an hour while I lay on my bed staring at the ceiling.

When I finally opened it, I had to sit down.

Inside: your grey hoodie, the one with the frayed cuffs and the paint stain on the sleeve from when we painted your room. A packet of the instant coffee I like that they don't sell here. A small jar of your mother's mango pickle, wrapped in three layers of plastic. A photo of us from the beach trip, the blurry one where we're both laughing too hard to look at the camera.

And a playlist, handwritten on a scrap of paper, twelve songs, each with a tiny note next to it. "For when you miss home." "For the metro." "For when the presentation goes badly (it won't)." "Don't skip this one." And at the bottom, in smaller letters: "For when you miss me: all of them."

You didn't know about the presentation. I hadn't told you. You just guessed I'd need it.

The hoodie still smelled like you. Like your detergent and that cologne you wear too much of. I put it on immediately, wet hair and all, and sat on my bed and cried in a way that was half sad and half something much warmer. Then I played all twelve songs, in order, without skipping.

We've been doing distance for a year now. Video calls are good. Texts are good. Voice notes are good. But there's something about a thing you can hold, a thing the other person held first, that a screen can't give you.

I wear the hoodie every night now. My roommate has stopped asking. The smell is fading, slowly, a little more each week, and I find myself rationing it, wearing it only after bad days.

I texted you this morning: "The smell is fading. Send another one."

You replied in four seconds: "Already packed."

title: Table for One
author: Anonymous, 27
content:
"Just one?" the waiter asked, and I said yes, and he said it again, louder, to the guy seating people. "One!" Like it was a confession. Like the whole restaurant needed to know.

I used to hate eating alone. I'd scroll my phone the whole time so nobody would think I'd been stood up. I'd order whatever was fastest. I'd sit facing the wall if I could. I'd leave as soon as the bill came, like someone might catch me existing without company and report me to someone.

But I moved to this city eight months ago for work, and I don't know anyone. My colleagues are nice, but they have families and plans and group chats I'm not in. And you can only order delivery so many nights before the walls of a one-room flat start feeling closer than they did yesterday.

So last month I made a rule: once a week, I eat somewhere out, alone, and I don't look at my phone. Not once. Not even to check the time.

The first few times were awful. I didn't know where to put my hands. I read the menu four times. I was sure everyone was looking at me, thinking, look at that sad person. I finished in twenty minutes and practically ran out.

Then something shifted. Slowly, without me noticing when. I started noticing things instead. The couple by the window who share dessert without asking each other, just two spoons, one plate. The old man who comes every Thursday and orders the same dal and reads the same newspaper and tips exactly twenty rupees. The kid at the next table drawing on a napkin while his parents argue quietly. The way the light hits the street at 7:40, gold and pink, just before the shop signs turn on.

I started looking forward to it. My Thursday table. My small, quiet hour.

I'm still lonely. I won't pretend I'm not. Some nights it still sits on my chest like a cat that won't move. But I'm also learning that being alone and being invisible aren't the same thing.

Last week the waiter didn't ask "just one?" He just smiled, said, "Your usual table's free," and brought my order before I'd even asked.

That counts for something. That counts for a lot.

title: The Group Chat Moved On
author: Anonymous, 24
content:
There are 247 unread messages in the college group chat. I scroll through them sometimes, late at night, like reading the diary of a life I used to be part of.

The group is still named "Backbenchers Forever 🔥". Someone changed the photo last month to one from our farewell, all of us squeezed into a single frame, sweaty and grinning. I'm on the edge, half cut off. I don't remember who took it.

They're planning a trip to Manali. Photos from a wedding I wasn't invited to, probably because I haven't replied to anything since February. Inside jokes I don't understand anymore, references to things that happened after I stopped paying attention. Someone got a new job. Someone got a dog named Biscuit. Someone asked, weeks ago, "Where's Aditi these days?" and nobody answered, and the conversation moved on to whether Biscuit should get a jacket.

It's nobody's fault. That's what makes it hard. We didn't have a fight. There was no dramatic ending, no betrayal, no screenshot. We just graduated into different cities and different schedules and different versions of ourselves. The gaps between messages got longer. Days, then weeks, then months. Until one day the gap was all that was left.

I used to be the one who planned things. The birthday surprises, the late-night Maggi runs, the trip to Lonavala where the car broke down. I don't know when I stopped. Maybe when work got hard. Maybe when I started feeling like I had nothing interesting to say.

I typed a message tonight. "Hey guys, miss you all." Then I deleted it. Too simple. Then I typed a longer one, explaining, apologising. Deleted that too. Too much. Then I typed the first one again.

It's sitting there now, unsent, the cursor blinking like it's waiting for me to be brave.

Maybe tomorrow. Maybe they miss me too. Maybe they're all sitting there with unsent messages of their own, cursors blinking in the dark, each of us thinking the others have moved on.

Maybe loneliness is just a lot of people waiting for someone else to go first.

I press send. Then I put the phone face down and hold my breath.

title: Sunday, 4 PM
author: Anonymous, 30
content:
Sunday at 4 PM is the loneliest hour of the week. I don't know why, but everyone I've asked agrees. There's even a name for it, apparently. The Sunday scaries. That sounds too cute for what it actually feels like.

The morning is fine. You sleep in, make a slow breakfast, tell yourself you'll be productive. The early afternoon is fine too. Laundry, a show, a nap with the curtains half drawn.

But somewhere around four the light changes. It goes soft and gold and slightly sad, slanting across the floor at a low angle. The street outside gets quiet. And you realise the weekend is ending, Monday is coming, and you haven't spoken to a single person out loud since Friday evening. Not one. Your voice actually sounds strange when you clear your throat.

I used to fill that hour with noise. TV on, music on, scrolling through three apps at once. It didn't help. It just made the silence underneath louder.

Then, a few months ago, almost by accident, I started calling my grandmother at 4 PM on Sundays. Not because she's lonely, though she probably is. Because I am.

She always picks up on the second ring, like she's been sitting by the phone. She tells me about the neighbour's grandson who got into engineering, and the price of tomatoes, and how my cousin never calls. She tells me the same story about my grandfather and the bicycle almost every week. I tell her about work, simplified so she can follow. We repeat the same things every Sunday and neither of us minds.

Sometimes she sings a little, an old song from a film I've never seen. Her voice is shaky now. I don't tell her that. I just listen.

Last Sunday she said, "You sound tired, beta. Are you eating?" and I had to put the phone down on the bed for a second, because nobody else has asked me that in months. Nobody else has noticed. I said, "Yes, Nani, I'm eating," and she said, "Eat more," and I laughed with tears in my eyes.

The light still goes gold at four. It's still a little sad. I don't think that will ever change.

But now it's also the hour someone asks if I've eaten. That's enough to get me to Monday.

title: The Delivery Guy Knows My Name
author: Anonymous, 25
content:
Ravi delivers my food at least four times a week. He knows my name, my building's broken lift, the dog on the second floor that barks at everyone, and that I always ask for extra chutney.

Last week he said, "Sir, you're not eating out at all, huh?" It wasn't a judgement. He said it kindly, like an observation about the weather. But it landed somewhere deep, because he was right, and because he was the only person in this whole city who had noticed.

I work from home. My family is in another state, two flights away. My friends here are really just colleagues who live on Slack, green dots that turn grey at six. I have a gym membership I don't use and a neighbour whose name I've never learned even though we've lived across from each other for a year.

Some days the only voice I hear out loud is Ravi's, telling me to have a nice dinner. Then the door closes and the apartment fills back up with silence, and I eat in front of my laptop, watching a show I'm not really watching.

I didn't plan to become this person. It happened slowly. One cancelled plan, one skipped call, one "I'll go next weekend" at a time.

Yesterday it was raining hard, and Ravi was soaked when he arrived. Without thinking, I asked him how his day was going. He seemed surprised, like nobody had asked him that in a long time either. Then he smiled and told me about his daughter, who just started school and wants to be a pilot. She draws planes on everything, he said. The walls, her notebooks, his hand.

He showed me a photo on his cracked phone screen. She was wearing a paper aeroplane on her head like a crown, grinning with two missing teeth.

I gave him a towel to dry off and a cup of tea. He said he couldn't stay. He stayed for five minutes.

It was a small conversation. Nothing, really. But I thought about it all night. I thought about how many people pass through my day without me ever looking up.

This morning I knocked on my neighbour's door to ask about the water timing. Her name is Meena. She has a cat.

Maybe this is how you climb out of loneliness. Not all at once. One small conversation at a time, with whoever is standing at your door.

title: The 3:07 AM Replay
author: Anonymous, 23
content:
At 3:07 AM my brain decided to replay something I said in a meeting four years ago.

Not something important. A small thing. Someone asked me a question about a spreadsheet and I gave a slightly wrong answer, and a colleague corrected me, kindly, and everyone moved on in about four seconds. Everyone except my brain, which has apparently been storing this clip in high definition, with surround sound, for exactly this moment.

After that came the greatest hits. The text I sent in 2019 that I shouldn't have. The friend I stopped talking to and never explained why. The time I said "you too" when the waiter said "enjoy your meal." That time I waved at someone who was waving at the person behind me, and then pretended I was fixing my hair.

Then my brain moved on to the future. Am I wasting my twenties? Should I have taken that other job? Do my friends actually like me or do they just tolerate me? Is that small pain in my side something serious? What will I be doing in ten years? Will I be doing anything?

The thing about 3 AM is that nothing is actually wrong. The room is fine. The door is locked. Tomorrow is a normal Tuesday. But in the dark every small mistake feels like a verdict, and every unanswered question feels like an emergency that needs solving right now, immediately, before the sun comes up.

I've learned a few tricks over the years.

I keep a notebook by the bed and write the thought down, just to move it from my head to the paper. It looks much smaller in ink. I put on a slow song with no lyrics and count the fan's rotations. I name five things I can hear: the fridge, a distant dog, a bike on the main road, my own breathing, the clock. I remind myself that the version of me at 3 AM is a terrible narrator who always, always picks the saddest ending.

I don't believe her anymore. Not completely.

The sun will come up. It always does, every single time, without fail. The birds will start. The milkman will ring his bell. And none of this will matter by breakfast. I'll barely remember it by lunch.

I turn over. I close my eyes. 3:41. Good enough.

title: Forty-Two Open Tabs
author: Anonymous, 26
content:
It's 2:14 AM and I have forty-two tabs open.

Let me give you a tour. A master's program in a country I've never visited, with a deadline I've already missed twice. A recipe for sourdough I will never make. An article titled "How to know if you're in the wrong career," which I've read four times and still don't know. A one-way flight to Bali that costs more than my rent. Three apartment listings in a city I keep saying I'll move to. A guitar course I paid for in 2022 and finished one lesson of.

A YouTube video of a man building a cabin alone in the woods. I've watched it three times. I don't even like the cold.

A Wikipedia page about octopuses, which I don't remember opening but now know far more about than I ever needed to. Did you know they have three hearts? I think about that a lot. Three hearts and still they live alone.

This is what my late nights look like. Not sadness, exactly. Restlessness. The feeling that there's a version of my life running parallel to this one, a braver, more interesting version, who speaks French and wakes up at 6 AM and actually goes to the gym. And that if I just click the right link, find the right course, book the right flight, I can step through into it.

During the day I'm fine. I have a job that pays the bills. I have friends I see on weekends. My mother tells her friends I'm "settled." But at night, when the house is quiet and the screen is the only light, the parallel life gets very loud.

In the morning I'll close most of these. I always do. I'll make coffee and go to my job. It's fine, actually. I like my colleagues. The coffee is decent. The work is sometimes even interesting.

But I'll keep a few tabs open, quietly, in the corner of the screen. The master's program. The octopus. The cabin. Like windows in a house I haven't moved into yet.

Maybe that's okay. Maybe everybody needs a few open tabs. Not as plans. As proof.

Proof that you still believe you could become someone new.

title: The Ceiling Fan Knows
author: Anonymous, 20
content:
Our hostel room has a ceiling fan that makes a tiny clicking sound every rotation. My roommate can't hear it. He says I'm imagining it. I can't stop hearing it.

Click. Did I choose the right course, or did I just choose what my parents wanted? Click. Are they disappointed in me, or just tired? Click. Why does everyone here seem to know exactly what they're doing? Click. Why do I feel homesick for a home I couldn't wait to leave? Click. Will I ever feel like I belong anywhere?

I've spent so many nights watching that fan that I've started to think of it as a friend. A slow, squeaky, slightly wobbly friend. It's been there for every question I couldn't say out loud.

It heard me cry after the first semester results, quietly, into my pillow, so my roommate wouldn't wake up. It heard me practise what I'd say to my father on the phone, five different versions, none of which I used. It heard me laughing at 4 AM with my roommate about absolutely nothing, a joke about a professor's moustache that wasn't even funny but somehow was. It heard me whisper "I miss home" in October, when the weather turned cold and the mess food tasted like cardboard and my mother's voice on the phone sounded far away.

Everyone else seemed fine. That was the hardest part. In the corridors, in the canteen, on Instagram, everyone looked like they were having the time of their lives. Parties, trips, new friends, new relationships. I thought I was the only one lying awake counting clicks.

Last night my roommate couldn't sleep either. I could tell from his breathing. We lay there in the dark for a long time without saying anything. Then he said, very quietly, "Do you ever feel like everyone else got a manual and we didn't?"

And I laughed so hard I had to sit up. Because that was the exact thought I'd been having for a year, almost word for word.

We talked until five. About home, about our parents, about how scared we both were all the time. He told me he hears the fan clicking too. He'd just been pretending he didn't.

Turns out the fan wasn't the only one listening. Turns out nobody got the manual.

title: Notes App, Drafts Folder
author: Anonymous, 28
content:
My Notes app has a folder called "Drafts" and nobody can ever see it. It has a lock on it. It's the most honest place I own.

Inside: a birthday message to my father that's much longer and softer than the "Happy birthday Papa 🎂" I actually sent. It talks about the time he taught me to ride a cycle and ran behind me for an hour in the heat, and how I never thanked him. It says I'm sorry for the things I said when I was nineteen. It says I see him getting older and it scares me.

An apology to a friend from 2021 that I rewrote eleven times and never sent. Each version is shorter than the last. The final one just says "I'm sorry. I miss you." I still haven't sent it.

A resignation letter for a job I didn't quit. A list of baby names, from a relationship that ended. A rant about my landlord that is honestly quite funny. A list titled "things I'm proud of" that I started on a bad night and add to on worse ones. It has thirty-two things on it now. Some are big. Some are "drank water today." Both count.

There's also a poem. It's not good. I wrote it at 1:30 AM after a party where I felt invisible in a room full of people. It has the line "I was loud enough to be in the photos but too quiet to be remembered," and every time I read it I want to delete it, and every time I don't. Because it's true, and I wrote it, and nobody else has to see it.

Late at night I'm a writer. I'm brave. I say everything I mean, exactly the way I mean it. During the day I'm a person who says "I'm good, you?" and "haha yeah" and "no worries," and smiles in meetings, and keeps everything folded up small.

I've been thinking about sending one of the drafts. Just one. Not the poem. Maybe the one to my father. His birthday is next month. He's sixty-two.

I opened it again tonight. I fixed one typo. I added one line at the end: "Thank you for running behind the cycle."

Maybe it's time the night version of me got to speak in daylight.
